2D Gaussian kernel smoothing by FFT, with reflected boundaries

Source: R/kernel-smoothing.R
ker.smooth.2D.fft.Rd

Smooths a matrix z sampled on an equally-spaced x/y grid with a separable Gaussian kernel of standard deviations x.bandwidth/y.bandwidth, using an FFT.

Usage

ker.smooth.2D.fft(x, y, z, x.bandwidth, y.bandwidth)

Arguments

x, y

Numeric vectors of equally-spaced grid points for each dimension.

z

Numeric matrix of values on the x by y grid (nrow(z) == length(x), ncol(z) == length(y)).

x.bandwidth, y.bandwidth

Standard deviations of the Gaussian smoothing kernel along x and y.

Value

A numeric matrix of dimension (length(x)+1) x (length(y)+1): the smoothed values at the points halfway between successive x (and y), and half a grid step beyond the first and last. When x and y are the midpoints of histogram bins, as from hist.weighted.2D(), these are the bin edges.

Details

Note that despite the shared "fft" in the name, this extends z by reflection in both dimensions, whereas the 1D ker.smooth.fft() extends periodically — appropriately so, since this one smooths the spatial triggering kernel (not periodic) and that one smooths the weekly and monthly background components (periodic). See ker.smooth.fft().

References

D'Angelo et al. (2024); see spHawkes-package.

Examples

# Smooth a single spike at the origin; the result, one more row and column
# than the input, is centred on the spike
g <- seq(-1000, 1000, by = 100)
z <- matrix(0, length(g), length(g))
z[11, 11] <- 1
smooth <- ker.smooth.2D.fft(g, g, z, x.bandwidth = 200, y.bandwidth = 200)
dim(smooth)
#> [1] 22 22
# The largest values sit half a step either side of the spike
edges <- c(g - 50, max(g) + 50)
peak <- which(smooth > max(smooth) * (1 - 1e-9), arr.ind = TRUE)
edges[unique(peak[, 1])]
#> [1] -50  50
